variants.name: ASP.NET Core scoped service with EF Core transaction
variants.implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the structure: register the service with AddScoped (one instance per request scope), inject its repositories and the DbContext by constructor, and register the DbContext with AddDbContext - scoped by default, so it is one unit of work per request. EF Core already wraps each SaveChanges in a transaction; an explicit DbContext.Database.BeginTransaction/Commit pair is only needed when several SaveChanges calls must commit or roll back together. Choose the ambient TransactionScope variant when the operation must span several contexts or resources, and fall back to a hand-wired service (constructing its context directly) in console tools, migrations and tests where no request scope exists.
pitfalls: A scoped DbContext resolved from a singleton becomes a de-facto singleton: resolve request-scoped services from the request scope, never capture them in a long-lived service.
Several SaveChanges calls without an explicit transaction commit independently, so a failure after the first one leaves a partially applied operation.

variants.name: Ambient System.Transactions scope (classic .NET)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic .NET Framework realization wraps the whole operation in a System.Transactions.TransactionScope: the transaction is ambient and thread-bound, every ADO.NET/EF call inside the scope enlists automatically, and scope.Complete() is the only commit - without it the scope rolls back. It remains the tool for an operation that spans several contexts or resources, but it depends on provider support (EF Core delegates to the provider and some providers ignore System.Transactions) and it escalates to a distributed transaction when a second resource enlists.
pitfalls: Forgetting scope.Complete() silently rolls the whole operation back even though every call succeeded.
Async methods must flow the transaction explicitly (TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled); otherwise each await leaves the ambient transaction behind.
Enlisting a second resource promotes the transaction to a distributed one, which is commonly disabled in cloud and container environments.
